'''Mbabaram''' (Barbaram) is an [[language death|extinct]] [[Australian Aboriginal languages|Australian Aboriginal language]] of north [[Queensland]], traditionally spoken by the [[Mbabaram people]]. [[R. M. W. Dixon]] described his hunt for a native speaker of Mbabaram in his book ''Searching for Aboriginal Languages: Memoirs of a Field Worker''. Most of what is known of the language is from Dixon's field research with speaker Albert Bennett.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dixon |first=Robert. M. W. |title=Searching for Aboriginal Languages: Memoirs of a Field Worker |publisher=University of Chicago Press |year=1989 |isbn=978-0226154305 |edition=2nd |language=en}}</ref>

Recordings are held in the audio collection of the [[Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Collections {{!}} AIATSIS corporate website |url=https://aiatsis.gov.au/collections/item/S0000265 |access-date=2026-03-12 |website=aiatsis.gov.au}}</ref>

==Classification==
Mbabaram is a [[Pama–Nyungan languages|Pama-Nyungan]] language, specifically belonging to the [[Paman languages|Paman]] group.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Glottolog 5.3 - Mbabaram |url=https://glottolog.org/resource/languoid/id/mbab1239 |access-date=2026-03-12 |website=glottolog.org}}</ref>

As part of his theory that the Mbabaram tribe (among others of the region) were of part [[Aboriginal Tasmanians|Tasmanian]] origin, [[Norman Tindale]] noted the Mbabaram language appeared strongly isolated, but [[Robert M. W. Dixon|R. M. W. Dixon]] stated the more reasonable view was that Mbabaram was very recognizably related to the languages of the region.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Dixon|first=Robert M. W.|date=1966|title=Mbabaram: A Dying Australian Language|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/611096|journal=Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London|volume=29|issue=1|pages=113-114|doi=10.1017/S0041977X00060833|jstor=611096|issn=0041-977X|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Geographic distribution==
Mbabaram was spoken by the [[Mbabaram tribe]] in [[Queensland]], southwest of [[Cairns]] ({{coord|17|20|S|145|0|E|region:AU-QLD}}).<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Dixon|first=Robert M. W.|date=1966|title=Mbabaram: A Dying Australian Language|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/611096|journal=Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London|volume=29|issue=1|pages=107|doi=10.1017/S0041977X00060833|jstor=611096|issn=0041-977X|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Their territory was bordered by the [[Walsh River]] in the north, and included the present localities of [[Irvinebank]], [[Petford]] and [[Lappa, Queensland|Lappa]].<ref name=":0" />

The nearby languages were [[Agwamin language|Agwamin]], [[Djangun language|Djangun]] ([[Kuku-Yalanji language|Kuku-Yalanji]]), [[Muluridji language|Muluridji]] ([[Kuku-Yalanji language|Kuku-Yalanji]]), [[Djabugay language|Djabugay]], [[Yidiny language|Yidiny]], [[Ngadjan language|Ngadjan]] ([[Dyirbal language|Dyirbal]]), [[Mamu language|Mamu]] ([[Dyirbal language|Dyirbal]]), [[Jirrbal language|Jirrbal]] ([[Dyirbal language|Dyirbal]]), [[Girramay language|Girramay]] ([[Dyirbal language|Dyirbal]]), and [[Warungu language|Warungu]]. Each language was [[Mutual intelligibility|mutually intelligible]] with at least its immediate neighbours, but Mbabaram was not mutually intelligible with any of them. Because of the difficulty of the language for other tribes, Mbabaram speakers would tend to learn their languages rather than the other way round.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Dixon|first=Robert M. W.|date=1966|title=Mbabaram: A Dying Australian Language|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/611096|journal=Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London|volume=29|issue=1|pages=108|doi=10.1017/S0041977X00060833|jstor=611096|issn=0041-977X|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

===Phonological history===
====Vowels====
Mbabaram would have originally had three vowels, {{IPA|/i/}}, {{IPA|/a/}} and {{IPA|/u/}}, with a [[Vowel length|length distinction]] in the initial, stressed syllable. Several changes occurred to add {{IPA|/ɛ/}}, {{IPA|/ɨ/}} and {{IPA|/ɔ/}} to the system:<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Dixon |first=Robert M. W. |title=Australian languages: their nature and development |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2002 |isbn=978-0521473781 |language=en|pages=599-600}}</ref>
*{{IPA|[ɔ]}} developed from original {{IPA|*/a/}} in the second syllable of a word if the word began with {{IPA|*/ɡ/}}, {{IPA|*/ŋ/}}, or {{IPA|*/wu/}}, e.g. {{IPA|*/ganda/}} > {{IPA|/ndɔ/}} "burn", {{IPA|*/gudaga/}} > {{IPA|/dɔg/}} "tame dog"
*{{IPA|[ɛ]}} developed from original {{IPA|*/a/}} in the second syllable of a word if the word began with {{IPA|*/ɟ/}}, e.g. {{IPA|*/djana/}} > {{IPA|/nɛ-/}} "sit", {{IPA|*/djiba/}} > {{IPA|/bɛ/}} "liver" (It may have also occurred with {{IPA|/ɲ/}} or {{IPA|/ji/}}, but no examples are known.)
*{{IPA|[ɨ]}} developed from original {{IPA|*/u/}} in the second syllable of a word if the word began with {{IPA|*/ɟ/}}, {{IPA|*/ɲ/}}, or {{IPA|*/j/}} e.g. {{IPA|*/djambul/}} > {{IPA|/mbɨl/}} "two", {{IPA|*/yundu/}} > {{IPA|/ndɨ/}} "you"
*{{IPA|[ɨ]}} developed from original {{IPA|*/i/}} in the second syllable of a word if the word began with {{IPA|*/ɡ/}}, {{IPA|*/ŋ/}}, or {{IPA|*/w/}} e.g. {{IPA|*/gabirri/}} > {{IPA|/bɨrr/}} "emu", {{IPA|*/wanji/}} > {{IPA|/njɨb/}} "what"
The first consonant and vowel of each word was then dropped,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dixon |first=Robert M. W. |title=Australian languages: their nature and development |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2002 |isbn=978-0521473781 |language=en|pages=631}}</ref> leaving the distribution of {{IPA|/ɔ ɛ ɨ/}} unpredictable.

=== Word for "dog" ===
Mbabaram is famous in linguistic circles for a striking coincidence in its vocabulary. When Dixon finally managed to meet Bennett, he began his study of the language by eliciting a few basic nouns; among the first of these was the word for "dog". Bennett supplied the Mbabaram translation, {{lang|vmb|dog}}. Dixon suspected that Bennett had not understood the question, or that Bennett's knowledge of Mbabaram had been tainted by decades of using English. But it turned out that the Mbabaram word for "dog" was in fact {{lang|vmb|dúg}},<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Dixon|first=Robert M. W.|date=1966|title=Mbabaram: A Dying Australian Language|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/611096|journal=Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London|volume=29|issue=1|pages=97–121|doi=10.1017/S0041977X00060833|jstor=611096|issn=0041-977X|url-access=subscription}}</ref> pronounced almost identically to the [[Australian English]] word (compare true cognates such as [[Yidiny language|Yidiny]] {{lang|yii|gudaga}}, [[Dyirbal language|Dyirbal]] {{lang|dbl|guda}}, [[Djabugay language|Djabugay]] {{lang|dyy|gurraa}} and [[Guugu Yimithirr language|Guugu Yimidhirr]] {{lang|kky|gudaa}}, for example<ref>{{cite book |last=Black |first=Paul |editor1-last=Bowern |editor1-first=Claire |editor2-last=Koch |editor2-first=Harold James |title=Australian languages: classification and the comparative method |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rmvmCvs9zQcC&q=Yidiny+dog&pg=PA264 |access-date=2010-01-08 |series=Amsterdam Studies in the Theory and History of Linguistic Science. Series 4, Current Issues in Linguistic Theory |volume=249 |year=2004 |publisher=John Benjamins |isbn=978-1-58811-512-6 |page=264 |chapter=The Failure of the Evidence of Shared Innovations in Cape York peninsula}}</ref>). The similarity is a complete coincidence: the English and Mbabaram languages developed on opposite sides of the planet over the course of tens of thousands of years. This and other [[false cognate]]s have been cited by typological linguist [[Bernard Comrie]] as a caution against deciding that languages are related based on a small number of lexical comparisons.<ref name="Comrie intro">{{cite book | last=Comrie | first=Bernard | title=The World's Major Languages | chapter=Introduction | publisher=Routledge | publication-place=Milton Park, Abingdon, Oxon; New York, NY|year=1987| doi=10.4324/9781315644936-1 | page=6| isbn=978-1-315-64493-6 }}</ref>
